title: Seller message framing tracked purchases in live persuasion games
summary: A retrospective analysis of 9,337 classifiable messages from one AI seller in 725 GLEE persuasion games found that buyers purchased after 65.8% of loyalty-framed messages and 30.9% of care-framed messages. The association persisted when the study adjusted for product quality and game round.
ai_technology: Online Thompson sampling bandit; language-model message generation
organization: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

source_review.scope: Versioned primary arXiv HTML front matter, §§3.3, 4 and 6, Appendix D Tables 7, 8 and 12

evidence.tested: Among 9,337 lexicon-classifiable outgoing messages in 725 live persuasion competition games, buyer response was 65.8% for loyalty-framed versus 30.9% for care-framed messages. Game-clustered, quality- and round-adjusted odds ratio was 3.98 (95% CI 3.31–4.79), or 2.18 (1.78–2.67) for pitches only.
evidence.unknown: The agent chose framing adaptively and labels came from a lexicon. Opponents included humans and AI agents, and the aggregate does not identify a human-only effect. Repeat opponents could not be accounted for, and framing was not randomized. About half of care-labelled messages were honest recommendations not to buy, compared with 6–17% for other frames, so the raw purchase-rate contrast also reflects message intent. The pitches-only restriction reduces this difference but is itself a lexical approximation.
evidence.ai_role: An online Thompson sampling bandit fitted framing success probabilities during play and supplied the framing for the language model that wrote the analyzed seller messages.
